# Acute liver failure

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Gastroenterology > Diseases of the liver > Acute liver failure*

[Original Article Link](/library/zr0rPh)

---

## Summary

Acute <u>liver</u> failure (ALF) is a severe condition characterized by rapidly progressive <u>liver</u> injury, <u>hepatic encephalopathy</u>, and impaired synthetic function, which results in <u>coagulopathy</u>. The most common causes are infections (e.g., viral <u>hepatitis</u>) and <u>acetaminophen toxicity</u>. <u>Signs of hepatic encephalopathy</u> may be accompanied by <u>jaundice</u> and nonspecific symptoms such as <u>nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u>, and fatigue. The diagnosis is confirmed by identifying an elevation of <u>liver chemistries</u> and an altered <u>coagulation panel</u> in patients with <u>encephalopathy</u>. Clinicians should maintain a high index of suspicion and aim to confirm the diagnosis as quickly as possible in order to start management early. Most patients with ALF are critically ill and require admission to a critical care unit. The prognosis is usually poor, and most patients require urgent <u>liver transplantation</u> as definitive treatment.




![Acute liver failure fact sheet](media/p9ldnm63d5zivlzwyam287bk.jpg)

## Definitions

* Acute <u>liver</u> failure (ALF)

* Rapidly progressive and severe <u>acute liver injury</u> lasting ≤ 26 weeks associated with <u>coagulopathy</u> and <u>encephalopathy</u> in individuals without previous hepatic disease  [[1]](/library/xmWE3N0)

* Subtypes are defined by the time it takes for <u>encephalopathy</u> to develop after the onset of other symptoms, e.g., <u>jaundice</u>.  [[1]](/library/xmWE3N0)[[2]](/library/dOXory)

* Hyperacute: ≤ 1 week

* Acute: 1–3 weeks

* Subacute: 3–26 weeks

* Acute liver injury: markers of <u>liver</u> injury (<u>elevated transaminases</u> with or without <u>hyperbilirubinemia</u>) and impaired <u>liver function</u> (i.e., <u>coagulopathy</u>) in patients with no <u>encephalopathy</u> and no <u>chronic liver disease</u>  [[3]](/library/alXQvy)[[4]](/library/9xWNAn0)





> [!TIP]
> Hyperacute presentations of acute <u>liver</u> failure carry a high risk of <u>cerebral edema</u> and are primarily seen in <u>acetaminophen toxicity</u>, viral <u>hepatitis</u> from <u>hepatitis A</u> and E, and <u>ischemic liver injury</u>. [[1]](/library/xmWE3N0)

---

## Etiology

* <u>Idiopathic</u> (20–45% of cases) [[5]](/library/spXtI_)

* <u>Hepatotoxic</u> drugs and supplements [[1]](/library/xmWE3N0)

* <u>Acetaminophen toxicity</u> (most common cause in the US) [[6]](/library/-pWDHm0)

* See “<u>Drug induced liver injury</u>” for other common causative agents.

* Infection [[1]](/library/xmWE3N0)

* <u>Acute viral hepatitis</u>

* <u>HAV infection</u>, <u>HBV infection</u>, or <u>HEV infection</u>

* <u>HBV</u>-<u>HDV</u> <u>coinfection</u> or <u>superinfection</u>

* Other viral infections (rare): <u>CMV</u>, <u>EBV</u>, <u>HSV</u>, <u>VZV</u>, or <u>adenovirus</u>

* <u>Toxoplasmosis</u> (e.g., in transplant recipients) [[7]](/library/YoWn0m0)

* Other <u>exogenous</u> toxins: e.g., <u>mushroom poisoning</u>, <u>aflatoxin</u>, <u>alcohol</u>  [[1]](/library/xmWE3N0)[[8]](/library/boWH0m0)

* Miscellaneous [[1]](/library/xmWE3N0)

* Vascular disorders: e.g., <u>Budd-Chiari syndrome</u>, <u>ischemic hepatitis</u>

* <u>Pregnancy</u>-related disorders: e.g., <u>HELLP syndrome</u>, <u>acute fatty liver of pregnancy</u>

* Inherited or autoimmune conditions: e.g., <u>Wilson disease</u>, <u>autoimmune hepatitis</u>

* Malignant infiltration: e.g., <u>lymphoma</u>, <u>metastases</u>

---

## Clinical features

Presentation is mostly nonspecific; clinicians should maintain a high index of suspicion in patients who acutely develop the following symptoms: [[2]](/library/dOXory)[[3]](/library/alXQvy)[[9]](/library/sGXt0-)




* <u>Signs of hepatic encephalopathy</u> (e.g., <u>altered level of consciousness</u>, <u>asterixis</u>)

* <u>Symptoms of cerebral edema</u>  [[10]](/library/f8XkN-)

* <u>Nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u>

* Fatigue, <u>lethargy</u>, <u>malaise</u>

* <u>Jaundice</u>, <u>pruritus</u>

* <u>Anorexia</u>

* Abdominal <u>pain</u>: may be located in the <u>RUQ</u> or diffuse, secondary to <u>ascites</u>

* Features of the underlying etiology (e.g., <u>Kayser-Fleischer rings</u> in <u>Wilson disease</u>)





> [!WARNING]
> In hyperacute <u>liver</u> failure, <u>jaundice</u> is usually minimal and the predominant presentation is <u>encephalopathy</u>, which can delay diagnosis and management.




> [!TIP]
> <u>ACLF</u> (e.g., <u>decompensated cirrhosis</u>) and ALF have many overlapping clinical features; features unique to <u>ACLF</u> include <u>signs of portal hypertension</u>, <u>variceal hemorrhage</u>, and <u>hepatorenal syndrome-acute kidney injury</u>. [[1]](/library/xmWE3N0)

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[1]](/library/xmWE3N0)




* Obtain initial <u>laboratory studies</u> to support the diagnosis and assess severity based on organ dysfunction.

* ALF is confirmed if all of the following are present:

* <u>Encephalopathy</u>

* Abnormal <u>liver chemistries</u>

* <u>Coagulopathy</u> (<u>INR</u> > 1.5)

* Obtain imaging to rule out alternative diagnoses, e.g., head CT to rule out other causes of <u>encephalopathy</u>.

* Identify the underlying cause.

* Consider causes based on <u>patient history</u>, e.g., <u>alcohol-associated hepatitis</u>, <u>metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease</u>, or <u>drug-induced liver injury</u>.

* Obtain additional <u>laboratory studies</u> based on clinical suspicion.

* <u>Liver biopsy</u> may be considered if the underlying cause remains unclear.





> [!TIP]
> ALF diagnosis requires the presence of abnormal <u>liver chemistries</u>, <u>coagulopathy</u> (<u>INR</u> > 1.5), and <u>encephalopathy</u>. [[1]](/library/xmWE3N0)




### Initial studies [[1]](/library/xmWE3N0)




#### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[9]](/library/sGXt0-)




* <u>CMP</u>

* <u>Liver chemistries</u>: <u>elevated transaminases</u>, <u>hyperbilirubinemia</u>

* <u>Hypoglycemia</u>

* <u>Electrolytes</u>: may show various disturbances, e.g., <u>hyponatremia</u>, <u>hypokalemia</u>, <u>hypophosphatemia</u>

* <u>Renal function tests</u>: ↑ <u>BUN</u> and <u>creatinine</u> in patients with <u>acute kidney injury</u> or <u>hepatorenal syndrome</u>

* <u>Coagulation panel</u>

* <u>Viscoelastic hemostatic assay</u>: preferred alternative to <u>INR</u> for determining bleeding risk  [[12]](/library/AkdRqJ0)[[13]](/library/etdxc70)

* Prolonged <u>prothrombin time</u> (<u>INR</u> ≥ 1.5)

* Presence of other derangements (e.g., <u>hypofibrinogenemia</u>) is variable

* <u>CBC</u>

* <u>Platelet count</u> typically â¤ 150,000/mmÂ³

* Other findings may be present depending on the underlying cause (e.g., <u>leukopenia</u> in some viral infections)

* <u>Blood gas analysis</u> 

* Acid-base status can vary between <u>acidosis</u> , <u>mixed acid-base disorder</u>, and <u>alkalosis</u> , depending on the underlying etiology [[14]](/library/j8X_m-)

* <u>Lactate</u>: commonly elevated; marker of severe disease

* Other

* Serum <u>ammonia</u> (preferably arterial): frequently elevated; values > 150 Î¼mol/L are associated with a higher risk of <u>increased ICP</u>.

* <u>LDH</u>: typically elevated in early stages of acute <u>liver</u> failure

* Blood and <u>urine cultures</u>

* <u>Type and screen</u>





#### Imaging [[1]](/library/xmWE3N0)




* CT head: Obtain initially to rule out alternative <u>causes of altered mental status</u>.

* Abdominal <u>ultrasound</u> with Doppler: to assess <u>liver</u> damage  [[15]](/library/7pX4I_)

* <u>Ultrasound</u> findings

* Early: may include heterogeneous <u>hypoechogenicity</u> (sign of <u>necrosis</u>) and/or <u>ascites</u>

* Late: in patients who have been sick for at least seven days, may show a nodular surface, which can be mistaken for <u>cirrhosis</u>

* Doppler findings depend on the underlying cause, e.g., <u>portal vein thrombosis</u>, hepatic <u>ischemia</u>.

* <u>Chest x-ray</u>: to rule out cardiopulmonary complications

* <u>ECG</u>: to identify <u>dysrhythmias</u>

### Identifying the underlying cause [[1]](/library/xmWE3N0)[[16]](/library/fGXkAz)




#### Additional <u>laboratory studies</u>




* Viral studies

* All patients: <u>viral hepatitis panel</u> including <u>hepatitis E</u> <u>serology</u> with <u>IgG</u> and possibly <u>RNA</u> testing

* Consider <u>PCR</u> for <u>EBV</u>, <u>CMV</u>, <u>adenovirus</u>, and <u>HSV</u>.

* Consider <u>VZV</u> (<u>IgM</u>) in <u>immunocompromised</u> patients or those with a <u>vesicular</u> <u>rash</u>.

* Testing for <u>hepatotoxic</u> medications

* <u>Urine drug screen</u>

* Serum <u>acetaminophen</u> and <u>salicylate levels</u>

* Additional testing based on clinical suspicion

* Testing for more uncommon etiologies based on clinical suspicion, e.g.:

* Serum <u>ceruloplasmin</u> and <u>copper</u> studies for <u>Wilson disease</u> [[16]](/library/fGXkAz)

* Serum <u>IgG</u> levels and autoimmune markers ;   for <u>autoimmune hepatitis</u>

* <u>α-fetoprotein</u> for suspected <u>malignancy</u>

* <u>Pregnancy test</u> in suspected <u>HELLP syndrome</u>

* Serum <u>ferritin</u> in suspected <u>hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis</u> [[3]](/library/alXQvy)

* Hematologic studies (e.g., <u>blood smear</u>, <u>Coombs test</u>): may show abnormalities, e.g., <u>hemolytic anemia</u> in <u>Wilson disease</u> [[17]](/library/tpXXr_)





> [!TIP]
> In many cases, the cause remains unknown even after an extensive evaluation.




#### <u>Liver biopsy</u>




* Indications

* Unclear etiology

* The suspected underlying cause requires specific management (e.g., <u>autoimmune hepatitis</u>, <u>malignancy</u>).

* Findings: depend on the underlying cause; <u>necrosis</u> and <u>regeneration</u> are common.

* Complications: significant risk of bleeding





> [!TIP]
> The significant risks of performing a <u>liver biopsy</u> may outweigh the benefits, as most patients with ALF require a <u>liver transplant</u> regardless of <u>biopsy</u> results.

---

## Treatment

### General principles




* If indicated, start <u>NAC</u> as early as possible.

* If the underlying cause is known, initiate specific management.

* Assess candidacy for <u>liver transplantation</u> and, if necessary, transfer candidates to a transplant center without delay.

* Manage any complications, e.g., <u>cerebral edema</u>, <u>acute kidney injury</u>, or <u>coagulopathy</u>.





> [!TIP]
> Urgent <u>liver transplantation</u> remains the <u>standard of care</u> for ALF. [[9]](/library/sGXt0-)




### <u>N-acetylcysteine</u> (<u>NAC</u>) [[1]](/library/xmWE3N0)[[2]](/library/dOXory)[[9]](/library/sGXt0-)




* Indicated in all patients with ALF due to confirmed or suspected <u>acetaminophen toxicity</u>

* Consider in patients with ALF due to:

* Any other type of <u>drug-induced liver injury</u>  [[18]](/library/52WiRk0)[[19]](/library/PTWWIk0)

* Confirmed or suspected <u>mushroom poisoning</u>, e.g., <u>Amanita phalloides</u>

* Dosage and administration

* 21-hour IV <u>NAC</u> regimen DOSAGE

* 72-hour oral <u>NAC</u> regimen DOSAGE

* Consider extending therapy on a case-by-case basis depending on clinical and laboratory evaluations.

* Continue <u>NAC for acetaminophen overdose</u> until <u>NAC stopping criteria</u> are met. [[20]](/library/drWoT50)





> [!TIP]
> Administer <u>NAC</u> as early as possible if indicated, i.e., before <u>hepatic encephalopathy</u> becomes severe. [[11]](/library/cncaH10)




### Treatment of the underlying cause of ALF [[1]](/library/xmWE3N0)[[5]](/library/spXtI_)




* <u>Autoimmune hepatitis</u>: Consider a trial of <u>steroids</u> on a case-by-case basis, weighing the increased risk of infection against the likely benefit.

* Viral <u>hepatitis</u>: supportive treatment and antivirals, depending on the cause (e.g., <u>HBV infection</u>, <u>HSV</u> <u>hepatitis</u>)

* <u>A. phalloides</u> <u>poisoning</u>: Start treatment with <u>silibinin</u> (preferred) or <u>penicillin G</u>; consider <u>NAC</u>.  [[1]](/library/xmWE3N0)

* <u>Pregnancy-associated liver diseases</u>: Urgent delivery of the fetus is indicated.

* <u>Acetaminophen toxicity</u>: Start <u>NAC</u> and <u>management of acetaminophen overdose</u>.





> [!TIP]
> If the cause is medication- or substance-induced, notify the local poison control center.




### <u>Liver transplant</u> [[1]](/library/xmWE3N0)[[21]](/library/8pXOr_)




* Consider <u>liver transplant</u> in most patients, as a high <u>proportion</u> do not recover with supportive therapy alone.

* Use prognostic scoring systems to risk-<u>stratify</u> patients' need and urgency of <u>transplantation</u>.

* Commonly used scores

* <u>King's College criteria</u>: provides indications for <u>liver transplant</u>  [[5]](/library/spXtI_)[[21]](/library/8pXOr_)

* <u>MELD</u> (for patients over 12 years of age) or <u>PELD</u> (for pediatric patients): prioritizes patients waiting for a transplant

* For patients who require transplant: 

* Refer immediately to a transplant center.

* Obtain a <u>pretransplant evaluation</u> and <u>pretransplant infectious workup</u>.

### Management of complications [[1]](/library/xmWE3N0)[[2]](/library/dOXory)[[9]](/library/sGXt0-)




* <u>Encephalopathy</u>

* <u>Lactulose</u> DOSAGE may be considered in patients who are alert and do not require <u>respiratory support</u>.  [[3]](/library/alXQvy)[[23]](/library/48X35-)

* The benefit of <u>rifaximin</u> is unclear.

* Avoid <u>hyponatremia</u>.

* Metabolic and <u>nutritional support</u> 

* Optimize nutrition: for patients in a <u>catabolic</u> state, optimize weight-based protein intake enterally or via <u>TPN</u>.

* <u>Electrolyte repletion</u> and <u>treatment of hypoglycemia</u> as needed

* Avoid hypotonic fluids (may result in <u>hyponatremia</u>).

* Consider <u>glucose</u> infusion with a target <u>glucose</u> ∼ 140 mg/dL. [[2]](/library/dOXory)[[24]](/library/dHXo6z)

* Consider serial <u>CMP</u> monitoring.

* <u>Hemostasis</u> [[2]](/library/dOXory)[[24]](/library/dHXo6z)[[25]](/library/w7XhLz)

* <u>Correct coagulopathy</u> if there is active bleeding or a need for invasive procedures, usually using a combination of:  [[25]](/library/w7XhLz)[[26]](/library/Q8Xum-)

* <u>Fresh frozen plasma</u> (most common)

* <u>Recombinant factor VIIa</u>

* <u>Cryoprecipitate</u> (for <u>hypofibrinogenemia</u> < 100 mg/dL)

* <u>Vitamin K</u>

* <u>Platelets</u> (e.g., for severe <u>thrombocytopenia</u>)

* See “<u>Transfusion</u>” for dosages.

* Consider <u>stress ulcer prophylaxis</u> to prevent <u>GI bleeding</u>.

* Consult <u>hematology</u> for specialized management.

* Monitor <u>coagulation studies</u> and consider using <u>viscoelastic hemostatic assays</u>.

* Management of <u>kidney injury</u> 

* Optimize <u>hemodynamic support in patients with AKI</u>.

* Consider early <u>acute renal replacement therapy</u> (<u>CRRT</u> is preferred).

* See also “<u>Acute kidney injury</u>” and “<u>Hepatorenal syndrome</u>.”

* Monitor urine output and consider serial <u>renal function tests</u>.

* <u>Infection control</u> 

* Begin <u>infection control and prevention</u> measures based on individual risk (e.g., consider isolation).

* Screen for and start empiric <u>antibiotics for sepsis</u> if suspected.

* Monitor with frequent clinical assessments (e.g., <u>vital signs</u>, <u>qSOFA</u>).

* Consider serial biomarkers (e.g., <u>CBC</u>, <u>CRP</u>, <u>ESR</u>).
